story: Belgium has a famous habit of going without a government, once for 541 days. In 2025 it finally got one led, unusually, by a Flemish nationalist, Bart De Wever, whose party wants eventually to dissolve the Belgian state. His promise was to govern "like the IMF": cut a budget deficit that breaks EU rules, rework pensions and limit how long people can draw unemployment benefits (Brussels Times).

Working Belgium answered by walking out, again and again. On 12 March 2026, police counted about 80,000 people marching in Brussels in a general strike, with unions claiming over 100,000 (Euronews). Another nationwide strike on 12 May grounded flights and stopped trains, with 40,000 to 70,000 marching, many carrying pictures of De Wever labelled "pension thief" (Euronews). The anger centres on three things: a pension "malus" that cuts payouts for people who retire early, limits on automatic wage indexation, the system that raises pay with prices and matters more than ever with energy costs pushed up by the Iran war, and cuts to benefits. The unions want a tax on large fortunes instead. The government says it needs roughly €10 billion in savings and that the reforms are what every other European country has already done. It is a classic European fight over who pays for an ageing society, playing out in the capital of the EU.
briefing.power: A federal constitutional monarchy. King Philippe is head of state; the prime minister leads a federal coalition that must balance Dutch- and French-speaking parties, since governments need majorities on both sides of the language border. Regions and language communities hold large powers of their own.
briefing.holders: Prime Minister Bart De Wever (N-VA), leading the five-party "Arizona" coalition.
